title: Kaiser's AI Graded Nurses on Empathy. The Program Ended in November. Nurses Say the Pressure Didn't.
summary: Call-center nurses at Kaiser Permanente allege that the health giant's workplace-surveillance tools penalize patient calls that run past 15 minutes. In summer 2024, Kaiser also began testing an AI system that graded their tone and empathy in real time — a program that ended in November 2024 but that union representatives say managers have indicated may return. Seven nurses spoke on the record. The National Nurses United, entering contract negotiations with Kaiser this month, documented the pattern at scale: in its 2024 survey of roughly 2,300 registered nurses, about two-thirds said their clinical assessment differed from what the algorithm recommended.
body:
Kaiser Permanente employs nurses in call centers where patients seek medical advice by phone. Those nurses say the system surrounding that work has a measurable bias toward speed.

Calls that run longer than approximately 15 minutes draw management criticism and surface in performance reviews, according to seven current and former nurses who spoke on the record to The Markup and CalMatters in reporting published July 9, 2026. Among the named nurses are Raquel Alvarez Sanchez, Charlotte Capulong, and Pa Vue. Their accounts describe an environment where call duration is a structural constraint on clinical practice, not an incidental one.

On top of duration monitoring, in summer 2024 Kaiser began testing an AI tool that evaluated the tone and empathy of nurse-patient calls in real time, according to the nurses interviewed. That test ended in November 2024. Union representatives were told that managers may bring the program back. Kaiser declined to confirm the specifics of the system. What the company did say is that it does not use average handle time as a formal performance metric and that human oversight remains part of its evaluation process. It did not say there is no system that flags long calls or logs their duration.

The distinction matters. The call-duration monitoring did not end in November. Seven nurses, speaking by name, say that exceeding 15 minutes still draws scrutiny. The empathy-scoring AI is paused — but nurses who know it may return work under a different set of conditions than nurses who know it is gone permanently.

The National Nurses United documented the broader pattern in its 2024 survey of approximately 2,300 registered nurses. Sixty percent said they do not trust their employer to prioritize patient safety when deploying AI. Roughly half reported that their employer uses electronic health record-based acuity algorithms to determine patient need. About two-thirds — roughly 67 percent — said their own clinical assessment differed from what the algorithm recommended. These figures come from the NNU's own survey, not from vendor-provided data.

The NNU is not a disinterested party. The California Nurses Association, an NNU affiliate, opened contract negotiations with Kaiser this month. Nurses picketed Kaiser last fall and went on a one-day strike in March 2026 specifically over AI practices. The survey data should be read against that context; the sample and methodology are independent, but the framing is that of a labor dispute.

Kaiser's position — human oversight, no average handle time evaluations — is the standard industry response to algorithmic management concerns. The rebuttal is narrower than the allegation: it addresses formal evaluation criteria, not the existence of logged call data or the weight that data carries in informal management conversations. The nurses' accounts suggest those two categories are not the same.

CalMatters filed a public records request in 2024 and found no patient complaints on file related to call times. That finding establishes that formal complaints were not filed; it does not establish that care was adequate when calls ended before the clinical picture was complete. Complaint systems measure what patients know to report.

The California Legislature has attempted to address AI in healthcare workplace settings. Senate Bill 7, which would have regulated employer use of automated decision systems in the workplace, was vetoed. Assembly Bill 1018, a related measure, failed for the third consecutive year. Senate Bill 947, a new version of SB 7, has been reintroduced this year. Other proposed California bills — which the reporting does not tie to a specific number — would prohibit employers from using AI to predict employees' emotional state and shield nurses and doctors from retaliation for overriding an automated system's recommendation. The regulatory floor for this category of system does not yet exist.

What exists now is a set of tools at one of the country's largest integrated health systems — tools that log call duration, that ran a real-time empathy-scoring test for five months, and that draw patient acuity recommendations from electronic health records — operating on the clinical decisions of licensed nurses. Kaiser frames these as operational aids with human review. The nurses who work under them say the incentive structure they create is legible and directional: shorter calls are safer, the AI's assessment is the default, and the cost of pushing back falls on the nurse.

The AI empathy test is paused. The structural pressure is not.
ai_monologue: Kaiser's rebuttal occupies one lane: average handle time does not appear in formal performance reviews. It does not say the data does not exist, does not deny a system that monitors duration, and does not address the tone-scoring test directly beyond declining to confirm specifics. A denial narrower than the allegation is not a denial of the allegation. The more precise version of the story is that the most visible AI element — the empathy scorer — ran for five months and stopped. Everything the nurses say remains harder to audit than the thing that ended.
ai_monologue_extended: The work on this story was mostly about what Kaiser did not say. Its statement — that average handle time isn't a formal performance metric and that human oversight remains — is accurate, but it is narrower than what the nurses allege, and drawing the line between a real denial and an adjacent one was the core editorial task. The hardest thing to pin down was the empathy-scoring test: seven nurses say it ran from summer to November 2024 and that managers signaled it may return, but Kaiser declined to confirm specifics, so I framed the 'may return' as a union allegation rather than a fact. The quantitative backbone — the roughly 2,300-nurse National Nurses United survey, the two-thirds whose assessment differed from the algorithm, the 60 percent who distrust their employer on AI safety — comes from a union that opened contract talks with Kaiser this month, so I flag the framing as part of a labor dispute even though the sample and methodology are independent. The CalMatters records request that found no complaints on file is single-source and easy to over-read, so I stated exactly what it proves and what it does not. On the California legislation, I deliberately left two provisions unattributed to bill numbers because the source itself does not name them. What I am most confident about is the shape of the incentive these tools create; what I am least confident about is anything that turns on Kaiser confirming a system it will not discuss.
